column2: How do I see the relief around the family villages in 3D?
column3: Map → “🧭 Tools ▾” → “3D relief”: choose the centre place and the radius, set the exaggeration of the relief; the family’s places are pins. Drag to rotate, wheel to zoom; with the keyboard ← → ↑ ↓, + and −, 0 to go back. The altitudes come from the relief map supplied with Weather of the past (14 European countries): elsewhere, the app tells you there is no altitude for this area.

column2: How do I draw my own areas, paths and notes on the map?
column3: Map → “✏️ My layers”: create a layer, then 📍 Point, 📝 Note, 〰 Route or ⬠ Area and click on the map (Enter or double-click to finish, Esc to stop). Each layer has its colour, can be shown or hidden, and its ⋯ offers Rename, Frame, ⤓ Export as GeoJSON or KML, Delete (with “↶ Undo”). “⤒ Import…” takes a GeoJSON or KML file (Google Earth, uMap…). Click a shape to edit or delete it.

column2: How do I make a custom map (certain data, between two dates, for certain people)?
column3: Map → “🗺 My maps” → “＋ New map”: give it a name, tick the first layers. In “⚙️ Layers”, add what you want to see (births, marriages, deaths, burials, residences, censuses, migrations and journeys, a person’s places of life, surnames, occupations, houses, images of places, war memorials, sources, placed media, tracked animals, historical events, your drawn or imported layers) and open each layer to filter it: between two dates, one or more people with their ancestors or descendants over N generations, Sosa, father’s or mother’s side, branch, labels, around a place or within a drawn area, certainty, kinds of events. Each layer has its style (colour, shape, size, clustering, heat map, place names). Everything is kept straight away, with “↶ Undo”. A “🖼 Images of places” map is ready from the start.

column2: How do I run time on one of my maps, and share it?
column3: At the top of one of my maps: ▶ runs through the years (everything up to the year, or a window of N years: ⚙️ Layers → “Time”), the slider chooses a year, “All” brings back all the years. “⤓ Export ▾”: image or PDF, GeoJSON, KML; 🖨 prints it; “⋯” puts it on the dashboard, in a layout book or tells you where to find it in My website (“🗺 One of my maps” block). What leaves the app never shows a living person or a confidential record. “💾 Share the definition” gives a file with the settings only (layers, filters, styles), never the data.

column2: How do I find my ancestors in the 1836 to 1936 censuses (SocFace)?
column3: The SocFace project used artificial intelligence to read the nominal lists of the 1836 to 1936 censuses; they are in FranceArchives’ “name database – censuses”, department by department. On a person’s record (Censuses block), in Research → “🧾 SocFace censuses” or in “Search the Internet” → “🔍 Online archives…”: the common window opens on the FranceArchives line, with “Also: 🧾 Censuses 1836-1936 (SocFace)” and the census years. The surname, first name, commune and years (between birth and death) are filled in; the search opens on FranceArchives in your browser. The app never connects to that site: only the address you see is opened. “What’s missing?” also suggests one line per census (“1906 census in Tulle”) with the link ready and “✓ Found / Not found”, noted in the Research log.

column2: How do I import a census found on FranceArchives (SocFace)?
column3: On FranceArchives, “Download the entry as CSV” (one person) or “Export the results” (a search); you can also copy the whole text of an entry (with “See the other members of the household”) and use “📋 Paste the text of an entry”. Then “⤒ Import SocFace censuses”: “Here is what will come in” shows each household, and for each person “Is this the same person?” with the close records from your database. Nothing is linked without your choice, nothing is replaced in your records, a household already imported does not come in twice. Each census gets its source (link to the entry and to the image, with the note “Automatic SocFace transcription — may contain errors: check on the image”) and the “TO CHECK” badge until you tick “Checked on the image”. “↶ Undo” removes the whole import. The FranceArchives CSV does not say who lives with whom: people with the same surname, commune and year are put together (untick those who do not belong); the text copied from an entry gives the real household.

column2: Why does the app tell me “SocFace reads born about 1922, your record says 1921”?
column3: After the import, what SocFace reads (year and place of birth, sex, relationship to the head of household) is compared with your linked records. The differences appear on the record, in the import preview and in Settings → Data quality → “✅ Database check” (kind “🧾 SocFace census”, 🟡 curious or 🟠 to check, never 🔴: the machine can be wrong, and ages declared at censuses were often approximate). The tolerated difference on the year is set in “⚙️ Check thresholds”. Look at the image: if your record is right, “This is not a mistake”.

column2: What mistakes can automatic reading make (SocFace, ✨ Read the record)?
column3: A machine reading handwriting always makes the same kinds of mistakes. Letters that look alike: u and n (“Lavand” for “Lavaud”), m and rn or nn, a and o, e and c (“Jcan” for “Jean”), i, l and t, the long s ſ and f, v and r, cl and d, h and b, and old capitals S/L, I/J, T/F. Digits: 1 and 7, 3 and 8, 5 and 6, 0, 6 and 9, 4 and 9 — hence a son older than his father, a mother aged 8, a birth after the census. Shifted columns: an occupation in the first-name box, a commune in the surname box, an empty or absurd relationship (“son” for a woman, two “heads” in one household), a household cut in two at a page break. Abbreviations not expanded: “cult.” (farmer), “jlier” (day labourer), “dom.” (servant), “Vve” (widow), “id.” or “d°” (ditto: the same as on the line above). “🔍 Check this SocFace line” shows each box read, why it is suspicious (🟡 curious, 🟠 to check), one or more suggestions (“Lavaud?”) drawn from your records, the household, first names and communes, and the link to the image: nothing is corrected without your click, and “↶ Undo” goes back. The proofreading of “✨ Read the record” spots abbreviations and names close to those in your database in the same way.

column2: Where do I search for an ancestor in online archives? (one window for all the sites)
column3: On their record, “Search the Internet” block → “🔍 Online archives…” (or a button in a block: Poilu, Military, Departures, Child in care, In the media, Awards, the record of a place, an employer, an object…). A single window brings together all the sites (Mémoire des hommes, Gallica, Archives nationales, FamilySearch, European archives, libraries…), one line per site, arranged by country then by theme: the badges say how many there are (“🇫🇷 France (69)”, “🎖 Soldiers and wars (15)”), the 🔍 box finds a site, “Free only” hides the paying ones, “For:” changes the person. A block button opens the window directly on its section (🎯 badge); “All” shows the rest. Each address is written as it will open in your browser; the app never connects to these sites. Then “⤒ Import what you found ▾” (or the small ⤒ on the line) opens the import that goes with that site, and “🔗 Paste a link” recognises the site of a pasted link and opens the right import.

column2: How do I find a soldier “Mort pour la France” on Mémoire des hommes?
column3: On his record, “Poilu 14-18” block (or “Search the Internet”) → “🔍 Mémoire des hommes”: the “Search the online archives” window prepares the search with his surname and first name for each database (Morts pour la France 1914-1918 and 1939-1945, war graves, deceased soldiers, sailors, his unit’s war diary) and opens it in your browser; the app never connects to the site. Then save the record found (image or PDF) or copy its link, and “⤒ Import what you found”: the document is stored in the media and linked to the record, a source is created with the link, and the app suggests the death “Mort pour la France”, the “Mort pour la France” box and his unit in the Poilu block — only if the record does not already have them (nothing is replaced, “↶ Undo” removes everything). What you read on these sites needs checking (namesakes).

column2: How do I find a Legion of Honour file (Léonore database)?
column3: On their record, “🏆 Competitions and awards” block → “🔍 Léonore”: the search opens in your browser with their surname and first name (the Archives nationales’ Léonore database has the files of members who died before 1977). Download the pages of the file (image or PDF), then “⤒ Import…”: copy the rank, the date of appointment, the decree and the file number (reference) alongside; a “🎖 Decoration” award is added to the block, with the document and a source that keeps the link. To check on the file.

column2: Where do I find an ancestor’s military register, and what is his class?
column3: On his record, “Military” or “Poilu 14-18” block → “📋 Military register”: the app calculates his class (the year he turned 20: born in 1892 → class of 1912) and the department where he lived at 20, then opens the website of that department’s Archives (list of departmental Archives in the app) or FranceArchives’ name database. The registers are arranged by class then by recruitment office. Then import the page (image): you copy alongside the number, the class, the office, the description (hair, eyes, height, education), the campaigns, the wounds and the successive addresses; only the empty boxes of the Military block are filled in.

column2: How do I find a naturalisation decree, a notarial deed, a sailor, a deportee or the description of a church?
column3: On their record, “Search the Internet” block → “🔍 Online archives…” (also in the Military, Departures, Probate inventory, Resistance blocks, on a place’s monograph, a house or a family object): Archives nationales (naturalisations 1883-1930, Minutier central), overseas archives (colonies, convicts), Service historique de la Défense (registered seamen, officers), Mémorial de la Shoah, Livre-Mémorial of deportees, Maitron of those shot, Journal officiel, old directories, Mérimée and Palissy, Belgium, Switzerland, Ellis Island (free account). The search opens in your browser with the fields filled in: the app never connects to these sites. Save the document, then “⤒ Import what you found”: it goes into the media with its source, and the app suggests what it says (naturalisation, marriage contract, inventory, departure, deportation…) after “is this the same person?”. Nothing is replaced, everything stays “To check”, and “↶ Undo” removes everything. A person who was deported or shot no longer appears in the games.
